summary: This informational memo argues that concurrent or successive TCP connections between similar hosts can share part of their state, such as round-trip time estimates and congestion information. It was replaced by RFC 9040.

eli5.summary: Two friends on the same road tell each other how bad the traffic is instead of each finding out the hard way.

questions: what is a tcp control block
what is temporal sharing in tcp
subtitle: Why TCP connections between the same two hosts should share what they have learned about the path.

tldr.problem: Each TCP connection keeps its own state and starts from scratch, so many short or simultaneous connections to the same host repeat the same measurements and can interfere with each other.
tldr.mechanism: Share part of the TCP control block between connections to the same host, either across time (temporal sharing) or among concurrent connections (ensemble sharing), so new connections start with the MSS and round-trip time estimates already learned.
tldr.outcome: This informational memo was replaced by RFC 9040. It argues the case and sketches rules, and says the authors were still performing analysis and experiments.

today: RFC 2140 is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 9040, which is the place to look for the current text.

sections.title: The Case for Sharing TCP State
sections.content:
TCP keeps state for each connection in a data structure usually called the TCP Control Block (TCB). As originally specified and usually implemented, the TCB is kept per connection. This memo argues for sharing some of that state among similar connections, both successive ones and simultaneous ones.

The expected gain is better transient performance, especially for many short-lived and simultaneous connections such as those used by the World-Wide Web. The changes only affect how a TCB is initialized, so they do not change the long-term behavior of TCP once a connection is established. The goal is to keep backward-compatibility with existing implementations.
sections.eli5: Instead of every new phone call starting from zero, the callers remember what they already learned about the line.

sections.title: What Lives in a TCB
sections.content:
The memo splits the TCB into local process state (buffer and queue pointers) and per-connection shared state. The latter has macro-state, which describes the finite state machine (connection state, timers, flags, host numbers and ports), and micro-state, which maintains reliability and congestion control after the connection is established.

Some micro-state is tied to the pair of hosts rather than to the pair of applications. Some of it is clearly host-pair dependent, such as the MSS and the round-trip time (RTT) with its variance. Other parts, such as congestion window information and current window sizes, are host-pair dependent only in aggregate.
sections.eli5: Some of what a connection knows is about the two applications talking, and some is about the road between the two computers. The road facts can be shared.

sections.title: Temporal and Ensemble Sharing
sections.content:
The memo names two cases. Temporal sharing uses the TCB of an earlier, now CLOSED connection to a host to initialize a new connection to the same host. Ensemble sharing uses a currently active connection to initialize another, concurrent one.

Temporal sharing already exists in T/TCP, which caches smoothed RTT, RTT variance, the congestion avoidance threshold and MSS. The memo describes the SunOS 4.1.3 T/TCP extensions and the FreeBSD port, which cache only the MSS and RTT parameters. The MSS cache is updated whenever the MSS option is received. RTT values are updated when a connection closes, with the rule old += (curr - old) >> 2, and the default MSS is never saved.

For ensemble sharing, cached data should be updated as early as possible, because otherwise concurrent connections may open before any connection has closed and nothing is shared. The RTT cache would be updated by an rtt_update function whenever the RTT would have been updated in a single connection.
sections.eli5: Sharing can happen after one connection ends (the next one remembers) or while several are running (they swap notes as they go).

sections.title: Sharing the Congestion Window
sections.content:
Congestion window sharing is harder for concurrent connections, because they usually share a network path and its capacity. The memo reasons that the set might behave as if multiplexed before TCP, so the sum of current window sizes would stay constant. Current implementations start each new connection at one segment, which raises that sum. The memo says this can hurt when several connections share a highly congested link, such as trans-Atlantic Web access.

It lists three ways to initialize the window of a new connection among N current ones. The proposed option gives the new connection a fair share and takes it from the others, with the memo stating that this may or may not be the right function and that it should be examined further.
sections.eli5: When a new kid joins a group sharing a pizza, either they get a tiny bite, take a whole slice, or everyone gives up a little so shares are fair.

sections.title: Compatibility, Cost and Implications
sections.content:
Current TCP implementations do not use TCB caching, apart from T/TCP variants, so each connection measures its own RTT, MSS and congestion information. The memo notes that if one connection has a window of 4 segments, new ones still assume 1 segment, and connections can interfere with each other. It says analysis and experiments to validate its assumptions were being performed.

The main cost is maintaining the cached values. Sharing happens only at connection establishment and close to limit overhead, though sharing during a connection may help if cheap.

The memo suggests this could remove the need for application-layer multiplexing such as persistent HTTP, since it offers the MSS, RTT and handshake avoidance of T/TCP plus avoidance of slow-start restart. It also treats this state as per-path, so it is better handled at the network layer, and notes that TCBs could even be shared between hosts on a LAN.
sections.eli5: Most computers did not do this yet. The authors think it could make lots of small downloads faster without changing how big transfers behave.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says sharing may be open to denial-of-service attacks if not secured. For example, an application could open a connection and set its window size to 0, harming later connections between those hosts. Attacks on initialization-only parameters affect transient performance, though for short connections this can approach a denial of service.

The requirements are that all shared TCBs MUST be validated against default minimum parameters before use for new connections, and shared values MUST be limited to performance factors only, not things like TCP sequence numbers. TCBs modified by an application SHOULD not be shared without explicit permission, and sharing on a LAN SHOULD use authentication.
sections.eli5: If one friend lies about the traffic, the others could be misled. So everyone double-checks the notes before trusting them.
